newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian property sell-off turns new leaf.
newsitem.headline: Russian property sell-off turns new leaf.

text.p: Russia's privatisation programme, marked by shady under-the-table deals and public controversy, has entered a new era in which clear-cut capitalist competition looks set to hold sway.

Emerging market economists analysing recent sales of key enterprises said on Wednesday that a major structural shift was under way, fuelled by a new, cut-throat competition between domestic financial and industrial groups for control over firms.

The change, like most in Russia, has a political dimension. The government is now seen by some analysts to want to use privatisation to score voters' points by ensuring that groups winning state stakes in companies pay enough to allow the state to pay off a huge backlog of workers' salaries.
That imperative, both fiscal and political, requires Russia to sell companies in a more competitive and transparent way to attract the highest bids for those firms.

The political fillip of more competitive sales would come from voters associating timely payment of salaries with the reformist cabinet and its potential presidential contender an election due in 2000 -- First Deputy Prime Minister Boris Nemtsov.
"Privatisation is linked to a pay-off to the people, and that is politically very important in Russia," said Susanne Gahler, a vice-president at JP Morgan in London.

When he first masterminded the sell-off in 1992, First Deputy Prime Minister Anatoly Chubais, Nemtsov's ally and Russia's privatisation guru, sought only to shift state property into private hands as quickly as possible.
Mass privatisation through vouchers gave way to shares for loans schemes, in which the government awarded major stakes to insiders in exchange for cheap loans.
Now Chubais has larger fish to fry, including filling budget coffers to pay wages and pensions, increasingly with money raised by selling state stakes in companies.

"Two years ago, Chubais just wanted to make reforms irreversible," said Pavel Teplukhin, chief economist at Troika Dialog. "Now, he has political ambitions -- he wants to pay wages and pensions...and he may use privatisation to do this."

The change analysts described could lend Moscow's sell-off a new image after years of offering up companies worth potentially billions of dollars to a narrow group of interest-driven insiders at bargain-basement prices.
Russia's sell-off has still not put company ownership in wide, diverse hands.

The two most recent sales of state stakes in major companies were won by the same powerful commercial bank, and Russia has only a narrow circle of less than a dozen financial-industrial groups rich enough to bid for enterprises in the oil, metals, telecoms and other key sectors.

But the two sales mark a shift that could lead to more competitive bids among the groups, more Western investor interest in Russian companies, more money for the budget and more timely payment of voters' salaries, economists said.

"Privatisation has been very inefficient -- it hasn't attracted investment resources or new management," said Jochen Wermuth of the Finance Ministry's economic experts' group. "Now, we're looking at a new phase."
One Russian company has been on both sides of the fence.

Uneximbank, Russia's third largest commercial bank and politically well-connected, won, through an affiliate, a 38 percent stake in the Norilsk Nickel metals group on Tuesday with a $250 million bid said to be well below market value.
The Norilsk sale is one of the last from the controversial shares-for-loans scheme, in which insiders have always won.

But Uneximbank also led an international consortium that won a $1.875 billion, quarter stake in the Svyazinvest telecoms holding last month, a sale dubbed Russia's largest and most transparent but slammed by the Russian banks which lost.
Russian media controlled by the banks which placed the losing bid plunged the government into near-crisis by attacking the Kremlin for its choice in the auction.
But analysts said the fact that one bank won two profoundly different auctions was less important than the fact that Russian banks now had to compete, and not just lobby, in sales.

"The chances are high that Svyazinvest is going to be the new rule of the game," Teplukhin said. "The reasons are that we currently have several major financial groups competing with each other, which they weren't doing last year."
